lead: An operating system is designed, built and started in stages. Design sets goals and separates mechanism (how an action is done) from policy (what action is chosen). Implementation turns those choices into C and assembly code, linked into a kernel image. Building uses compilers, linkers and loaders. Booting uses firmware, a bootloader, the kernel and init or systemd to reach a login prompt. The same chain explains why a binary built for one OS often fails on another. Phones, laptops and servers all follow it.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 for boot-time hardware and interrupts and Chapter 1.7 for kernel structures.

sections.h3: Design goals and policy versus mechanism

blocks.text: An OS design starts with goals. User goals are convenience, safety and speed: a phone should unlock quickly and not lose photos. System goals are efficiency, reliability and easy maintenance: the kernel should use few CPU cycles and be fixable. These goals conflict, so designers choose trade-offs.

A key rule is to separate mechanism from policy. A mechanism is the how: the code that can switch the CPU between processes or set a timer interrupt. A policy is the what or when: which process runs next, or how long a time slice lasts. For example, the timer hardware and interrupt handler are mechanism; the scheduler's choice is policy. Separation lets one kernel serve a phone and a server by changing policy data, not rewriting mechanism. It also makes testing easier.

Design shows in structure, covered in Chapter 1.7. Monolithic kernels put most services in kernel mode for speed. Microkernels keep only minimal mechanism in the kernel and move policy and services to user processes for isolation. Each choice changes performance and reliability.

Implementation is mostly C, with small assembly parts. C gives direct memory access and predictable performance. Assembly handles instructions that C cannot express safely: switching stacks, enabling interrupts, entering kernel mode. The source tree is configured for a target machine by system generation (sysgen): selecting drivers, page size, scheduler options. This produces a kernel image, a file the bootloader can load.

A program becomes runnable in stages. A compiler turns each source file into an object file. A linker joins object files and libraries into one executable, resolving addresses of functions. A loader is OS code that reads the executable, assigns memory, and jumps to its entry point. Static linking copies library code into the file; dynamic linking leaves a reference to a shared library loaded at run time. The OS also exposes an API: functions such as read() and fork() with names and arguments. Behind them are system calls, described in Chapter 1.6. An ABI fixes the binary details: register use, stack layout, system-call numbers.

Applications are OS-specific because they depend on all three: API names, ABI conventions and executable format. A program compiled for Linux uses Linux system-call numbers and ELF; Windows uses different calls and PE. Source code can be recompiled; a binary usually cannot.
Booting turns a stored kernel image into a running system. The sequence has fixed jobs.

items: Power on. The CPU starts at a fixed address in firmware.
Firmware runs POST (power-on self-test), checks RAM and devices, then finds a boot device. On modern PCs firmware is UEFI; older PCs used BIOS.
The bootloader is a small program that knows how to read the disk and load the kernel. GRUB is common on PCs. It may show a menu and load an initial RAM disk with drivers.

Kernel load. The bootloader places the kernel image in memory and jumps to its entry point. Early kernel code sets page tables, starts interrupts and initialises drivers. This is the kernel, not the whole OS.
The kernel starts the first user process: traditionally init, today often systemd. It reads configuration and starts services.
Login prompt or graphical session appears.

blocks.text: Times are not fixed; a slow disk extends bootloader and kernel load. The figure shows one measured run: firmware 2 s, bootloader 3 s, kernel 4 s, init 1 s, total 10 s.

figure.caption: The four boot stages in order on one 10 s time line; the running total reaches 10 s at the login prompt. The bootloader and kernel load take 7 of the 10 seconds.

spec.aria: A bar from power on to the login prompt split into firmware 2 s, bootloader 3 s, kernel load 4 s and init 1 s, with marks at 2, 5, 9 and 10 seconds.

examples.question: A PC takes 2 s in firmware, 3 s in the bootloader, 4 s loading the kernel and 1 s in init. What is the total time to the login prompt? Draw the boot sequence.
steps: List the stages and times: firmware = 2 s, bootloader = 3 s, kernel load = 4 s, init = 1 s.
Add them in boot order: 2 s + 3 s = 5 s after firmware; 5 s + 4 s = 9 s; 9 s + 1 s = 10 s.
Draw the flow: Power on → Firmware POST (2 s) → Bootloader (3 s) → Kernel load (4 s) → init or systemd (1 s) → Login prompt (total 10 s).
examples.answer: The total time to the login prompt is 10 s.

traps: The bootloader loads the kernel; it is not the whole OS. Firmware is not the OS kernel.
Mechanism is how an action is done; policy is what or when it is chosen. Do not reverse them.
Compiling a kernel is not booting. Compiling creates an image; booting loads and starts it.
A linker joins object files into an executable; a loader puts that executable into memory. Do not swap the names.
An API is source-level names and arguments; an ABI is binary register and stack rules. An application binary depends on the ABI.

quiz.q: Define mechanism and policy in OS design.
quiz.a: Mechanism is the how: code that performs an action. Policy is the what or when: the choice of action or timing.

quiz.q: Why is a kernel written mostly in C with some assembly?
quiz.a: C gives low-level memory access, speed and portability; assembly handles privileged instructions such as mode switching, interrupt entry and stack switching that C cannot express safely.

quiz.q: A phone takes 1.5 s firmware, 2.5 s bootloader, 3 s kernel and 1 s init. Find total boot time.
quiz.a: Total = 1.5 s + 2.5 s + 3 s + 1 s = 8 s.

quiz.q: Why may a program compiled on Linux not run on Windows even on the same CPU?
quiz.a: It depends on system-call numbers, ABI register and stack rules, and executable format (ELF versus PE). These differ, so the binary must be recompiled or run under a compatibility layer.
It loads the kernel image from disk into memory and jumps to its entry point; it may also load an initial RAM disk.

quiz.q: What is the job of init or systemd after the kernel starts?
quiz.a: It is the first user process. It starts services, mounts configured file systems and brings the system to login or graphical target.

quiz.q: Firmware runs before the kernel. Give one job firmware does and one job the kernel does.
quiz.a: Firmware runs POST and finds a boot device; the kernel sets page tables, starts interrupts and initialises drivers. They are different layers.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern systems use UEFI Secure Boot, measured boot and A/B partition updates so a failed update can roll back. Bootloaders such as GRUB and systemd-boot read configuration, while embedded boards use U-Boot and a device tree to describe hardware. Reproducible builds and signed kernels are active industry topics. Search terms: UEFI, GRUB, U-Boot, device tree, reproducible build, A/B update.
